subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A newborn delivered with lateral traction on the neck due to shoulder dystocia has an arm that hangs limply at her side. The arm is adducted, medially rotated, extended at the elbow, and pronated, with the wrist flexed, a waiter's tip posture. The biceps reflex is absent.
question: Which portion of the brachial plexus is injured?
explanation_correct: Erb palsy results from traction or tear of the upper trunk (C5-C6 roots), as with lateral neck traction during difficult delivery or trauma in adults. It affects the deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and biceps (mnemonic Herb gets DIBs), so abduction, lateral rotation, and elbow flexion are lost. The arm hangs adducted, medially rotated, extended, and pronated, the waiter's tip posture.

explanation_incorrect.A: The lower trunk (C8-T1) is injured in Klumpke palsy, which causes claw hand, not a waiter's tip posture.
explanation_incorrect.C: The medial cord gives rise to the ulnar and median nerves; its injury does not produce the classic waiter's tip of Erb palsy.
explanation_incorrect.D: The posterior cord gives rise to the radial and axillary nerves; injury causes wrist drop or deltoid paralysis, not the full upper-trunk Erb pattern.
explanation_incorrect.E: The middle trunk (C7) injury does not produce Erb palsy; the upper trunk (C5-C6) is the classic site.

educationalObjective: Erb palsy is an upper trunk (C5-C6) traction injury producing the waiter's tip posture with loss of abduction, lateral rotation, and elbow flexion.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: An adult falls from a height and grabs a tree branch to break his fall, sustaining a traction injury. He develops weakness of the intrinsic muscles of the hand and a claw-like deformity of the fingers. Sensation is diminished along the medial forearm and hand. Shoulder and elbow movement are preserved.
question: Which nerve roots are most likely injured?
explanation_correct: Klumpke palsy results from traction or tear of the lower trunk (C8-T1 roots), classically from an upward force on the arm such as grabbing a branch to break a fall or upward traction during delivery. It paralyzes the intrinsic hand muscles, namely lumbricals, interossei, thenar, and hypothenar, producing a claw hand because the lumbricals normally flex the MCP joints and extend the PIP and DIP joints. Shoulder and elbow movements are relatively spared.

explanation_incorrect.A: C3-C4 roots are not part of the brachial plexus (C5-T1) and do not supply the hand.
explanation_incorrect.B: C5-C6 roots form the upper trunk; injury there causes Erb palsy with a waiter's tip posture, not claw hand.
explanation_incorrect.D: C6-C7 injury would affect the upper/middle trunk, not the classic C8-T1 Klumpke distribution of intrinsic hand muscles.
explanation_incorrect.E: T1-T2 is not the standard lower trunk; Klumpke palsy is specifically C8-T1.

educationalObjective: Klumpke palsy is a lower trunk (C8-T1) traction injury causing claw hand from intrinsic muscle paralysis.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 35-year-old woman has an apical lung tumor that invades the superior chest. She develops atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of her hand and weakness of finger flexion, along with pain, edema, and pallor of the arm. Radiographs show a cervical rib.
question: Which structure is compressed to produce this combination of neurologic and vascular findings?

options.text: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus and subclavian artery
Long thoracic nerve and lateral thoracic artery
Lower trunk of the brachial plexus and subclavian vessels

explanation_correct: Thoracic outlet syndrome results from compression of the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and the subclavian vessels, most commonly within the scalene triangle. Causes include cervical or anomalous first ribs and Pancoast apical lung tumors. Compression of the lower trunk produces Klumpke-like intrinsic hand muscle atrophy and weakness, while subclavian vessel compression causes ischemia, pain, edema, and color changes, explaining the combined neurologic and vascular findings.

explanation_incorrect.A: Upper trunk and subclavian artery compression would produce Erb-like shoulder and elbow weakness, not intrinsic hand wasting with vascular congestion.
explanation_incorrect.B: The middle trunk is not the typical site, and the axillary vein is not the vascular structure compressed in the scalene triangle.
explanation_incorrect.C: Long thoracic nerve injury causes winged scapula from serratus anterior palsy, not intrinsic hand wasting or vascular compromise.
explanation_incorrect.D: The posterior cord and brachial artery are not the structures compressed at the thoracic outlet; the lower trunk and subclavian vessels are.

educationalObjective: Thoracic outlet syndrome compresses the lower trunk and subclavian vessels from a cervical rib or Pancoast tumor, causing intrinsic hand wasting plus vascular symptoms.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 48-year-old woman undergoes axillary lymph node dissection as part of treatment for breast cancer. Postoperatively, the medial border of her scapula protrudes when she pushes against a wall, and she cannot abduct her arm above the horizontal position. Sensation is normal.
question: Which nerve was injured?
explanation_correct: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7, wings of heaven) supplies the serratus anterior, which anchors the scapula to the thoracic cage and allows abduction above horizontal. It is vulnerable during axillary node dissection and stab wounds. Injury produces a winged scapula, with the medial border protruding especially on pushing, and inability to abduct the arm above horizontal.

explanation_incorrect.B: The thoracodorsal nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi for extension, adduction, and internal rotation, not the serratus anterior; injury would not cause winging.
explanation_incorrect.C: The axillary nerve supplies the deltoid and teres minor and lateral shoulder sensation; its injury causes a flattened deltoid and loss of abduction from 15 to 90 degrees, not winging.
explanation_incorrect.D: The suprascapular nerve supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus; injury affects the first 15 degrees of abduction and external rotation, not scapular winging.
explanation_incorrect.E: The accessory nerve supplies the trapezius; injury causes difficulty with scapular elevation and abduction above 90 degrees, but not the classic winged scapula of long thoracic nerve palsy.

educationalObjective: Long thoracic nerve injury from axillary node dissection causes serratus anterior paralysis, a winged scapula, and inability to abduct above horizontal.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A student reviews the organization of the brachial plexus. She recalls that the five roots (C5-T1) form three trunks that pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles. She wants to identify which vessel accompanies the trunks in this scalene triangle and which vessel lies anteromedial to it.
question: Which pair of vessels correctly fills those two positions?

options.text: Subclavian vein between the scalenes; subclavian artery anteromedial
Axillary artery between the scalenes; axillary vein anteromedial
Internal jugular vein between the scalenes; common carotid artery anteromedial
Subclavian artery between the scalenes; subclavian vein anteromedial
Subclavian artery between the scalenes; internal jugular vein anteromedial

explanation_correct: The three trunks of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles, within the scalene triangle, while the subclavian vein passes anteromedial to the scalene triangle. This relationship is clinically relevant in thoracic outlet syndrome and in approaches to the scalene triangle.

explanation_incorrect.A: This reverses the relationships: the artery runs with the trunks between the scalenes, and the vein is anteromedial.
explanation_incorrect.B: The axillary vessels are more distal, beyond the first rib; it is the subclavian vessels that relate to the scalene triangle.
explanation_incorrect.C: The internal jugular vein and common carotid artery lie in the carotid sheath, not the scalene triangle; the anteromedial vein here is the subclavian vein.
explanation_incorrect.E: The internal jugular vein does not pass anteromedial to the scalene triangle; it is the subclavian vein.

educationalObjective: The brachial plexus trunks and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle scalenes; the subclavian vein runs anteromedial to the triangle.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: An infant who suffered shoulder dystocia has the classic waiter's tip deformity. The arm is held adducted, medially rotated, extended at the elbow, and pronated, with the wrist and fingers flexed. The biceps reflex is absent while the triceps reflex is preserved.
question: Which combination of lost muscle actions best explains this posture?

options.text: Loss of elbow extension and wrist extension only
Loss of shoulder abduction, lateral rotation, and elbow flexion
Loss of finger abduction and thumb opposition
Loss of elbow flexion and wrist flexion
Loss of shoulder adduction and medial rotation

explanation_correct: In Erb palsy from an upper trunk C5-C6 injury, paralysis of the deltoid and supraspinatus removes abduction so the arm hangs by the side, paralysis of the infraspinatus and supraspinatus removes lateral rotation so the arm is medially rotated, and paralysis of the biceps removes flexion and supination so the arm is extended and pronated. This produces the waiter's tip posture. The triceps (C7) is spared because C7 is not in the upper trunk.

explanation_incorrect.A: Loss of elbow extension (triceps) and wrist extension (radial) would indicate a posterior cord or radial nerve lesion; the triceps is spared here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Loss of finger abduction and thumb opposition indicates ulnar or median or lower trunk pathology (Klumpke), not an upper trunk lesion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Loss of elbow flexion and wrist flexion is not the Erb pattern; wrist flexion is not lost in Erb palsy and the posture is one of extension.
explanation_incorrect.E: Shoulder adduction and medial rotation are actually the preserved unopposed actions in Erb palsy, since the arm is medially rotated and adducted, not lost actions.

educationalObjective: Erb palsy from upper trunk (C5-C6) injury loses abduction, lateral rotation, and elbow flexion (Herb gets DIBs), producing the waiter's tip posture.
